units.title: Capitalization
units.recap: Experienced writers are stingy with capitals. Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from them, and titles used before a name — but not occupations, and not titles that follow a name or stand in for one. Kinship names capitalize only when they replace a personal name. Capitalize specific regions, not compass directions. Capitalize specific course titles, not academic subjects. Seasons stay lowercase.

errors.explanation: Occupations are not titles. Director, owner, coach, and (per AP) professor stay lowercase even before a full name.

errors.explanation: A formal title used in direct address is capitalized: “Will you review the transcript, Judge?” The more formal the title, the more likely the capital.

errors.explanation: Kinship names capitalize only when they replace a personal name (“I found out that Mom is here”). After a possessive — my mom, Joe's grandpa — they're lowercase.

errors.explanation: Compass directions are lowercase; specific regions are capitalized. “We live in the Southeast” but “the southeast section of town.”

errors.explanation: Seasons and seasonal data are lowercase: spring, summertime, the winter solstice, daylight saving time.

errors.explanation: Specific course titles capitalize (Economics 101); general academic subjects do not (constitutional law, history, philosophy).

items.prompt: Which title is capitalized correctly under the Blue Book's universal rules?
items.explanation: Here “yet” is a coordinating conjunction, which stays lowercase in a title (unless first or last). In “Not Yet Rich,” yet is an adverb — and adverbs are always capitalized.

items.prompt: In a title, which is always capitalized?
options: Articles (a, an, the) anywhere in the title
items.explanation: The Blue Book's near-universal rules: capitalize the first and last word, all nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, and verbs (including forms of “to be”). Articles, coordinating conjunctions, and “to” stay lowercase unless first or last.

errors.explanation: Don't capitalize “the” before a proper noun — unless it is an inseparable part of the official name, as in The Hague.

errors.explanation: Do not capitalize the first item in a list that follows a colon (unless it's a proper noun). Capitalize after a colon only when a full sentence follows.

units.title: Writing Numbers
units.recap: Always spell out a number that begins a sentence. Hyphenate compound numbers twenty-one through ninety-nine and all spelled-out fractions. Use commas in figures of four or more digits. Don't write both a dollar sign and the word “dollars.” Use noon and midnight rather than 12:00. Decades take an apostrophe before an omitted numeral (’90s), never between the number and the s.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Always spell out a number that begins a sentence — and note the hyphen in forty-three. (Recasting the sentence is the other good option.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Figures of four or more digits take commas every three digits, counting left from the decimal point.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Never pair a dollar sign with the word “dollars” — the sign already says it.

errors.explanation: “a.m.” already means before noon — “4:00 a.m. in the morning” is redundant. Same trap as “8 p.m. this evening.”

items.prompt: Which does the Blue Book recommend for clarity?
items.explanation: Use noon and midnight rather than 12:00 p.m. or 12:00 a.m. — readers genuinely mix those up.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The Blue Book calls “’90's” awkward. Put the apostrophe before the omitted numerals and nothing between the number and the s: the ’90s.

Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: When spelling out decades, don't capitalize them: the eighties, the nineties.

errors.explanation: Hyphenate only the fraction when the number stands alone: five and one-half feet. Hyphenate the whole string only as a compound adjective: a five-and-one-half-foot-long sign.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: For sums under a dollar, skip the decimal point and the dollar sign: sixty cents (or 60 cents).

items.prompt: Which is correct when writing out a number in words?
options: one thousand one hundred fifty-four dollars and sixty-one cents
one thousand, one hundred fifty-four dollars, and sixty-one cents
one thousand and one hundred and fifty-four dollars
items.explanation: No commas when writing numbers out in words; “and” is reserved for the decimal point, not for joining hundreds.

items.prompt: When a number must appear as both a figure and words, which order does the Blue Book give?
options: Add 73 (seventy-three) grams — figure first, words in parentheses
items.explanation: Whichever form you lead with, the parenthetical comes second. Both “73 (seventy-three)” and “seventy-three (73)” are acceptable; the parentheses never come first.

items.prompt: AP style spells out zero through nine; Chicago spells out zero through one hundred. What follows from that?
options: Pick the convention your chambers uses and apply it consistently
AP is correct and Chicago is wrong
Always use numerals to be safe
items.explanation: The Blue Book confines itself to rules all media agree on and says the rest is preference. Consistency is the actual rule. (This app's drills follow the Chicago-style practice used in the judicial corpus.)
